screens.title: What is cron and how does it work?
screens.narratorSegment: Cron is a background scheduler: a lightweight daemon that checks configured crontab entries and launches commands at the scheduled times. The daemon, often started as cron or crond by the system service manager, repeatedly examines crontab files and directories to determine which jobs should run. A job can be defined in a user crontab or in system locations like /etc/crontab, /etc/cron. d, or the cron.* directories. When cron decides a job should run, it invokes the command with a limited environment. That reduced environment is a frequent source of surprises: command names and environment variables you rely on in an interactive shell may not exist under cron. A concrete example is a backup script that runs fine when you execute it manually, but fails in cron because the script calls python without the full PATH; cron cannot find python. A common misconception is that cron inherits your full login environment — it does not. You must either use absolute program paths or explicitly set PATH and other needed variables in the crontab or inside the script. Key takeaway: cron starts jobs reliably, but you must control the environment and permissions so those jobs run as you expect.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is cron and how does it work?
Cron daemon and execution
A continuous background service that inspects crontab files and launches commands at matching schedules.
Definition
Cron is the system scheduler process that reads crontab entries and runs commands on the requested cadence. It does not grant an interactive shell environment.
Analogy
Think of cron as an unattended timer: it rings at scheduled moments and executes the action you configured, but it has only what you give it in the configuration.
Execution flow (annotated)
  • Daemon wakes on a schedule tick and evaluates all crontab sources.
  • If a job matches, cron spawns the command with a minimal environment and the configured user account.
  • Output is mailed to the user by default or must be redirected into logs.
Concrete example
0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh # Runs daily at 02:00 and executes the script as configured user
If backup.sh calls python without '/usr/bin/python', cron may fail to find it. Use absolute paths or set PATH explicitly.
Common mistake
Assuming cron uses your interactive PATH. It doesn't.
Key takeaway
Always control environment and permissions for jobs run by cron.

screens.title: User crontab: commands and safe editing
screens.narratorSegment: Each user can maintain their own crontab file using the crontab utility; you should not edit files in /var/spool/cron/tabs directly. The key commands are crontab -e to edit (which creates the crontab if missing), crontab -l to list entries, and crontab -r to remove the current user's crontab. As root you may use crontab -u username -e to edit another user's crontab. A safe editing workflow is to run crontab -e, add your entry using absolute paths and explicit redirection for logs, then save. Verify with crontab -l and inspect any log files you redirected output into. A common misconception is that crontab -e uses your preferred editor without checks; it does, but a syntax error in a saved crontab can stop jobs from being installed, so always validate the entry format. Example: adding */5 * * * * /home/user/cron_scripts/check_disk. sh will run the script every five minutes. After editing, check the log file after 5–10 minutes to confirm that the job executed, and if it did not, check PATH, permissions, and the cron daemon status. This process gives you control over per-user automation without root access to system crontabs.

content.html:
Definition › User crontab: commands and safe editing
crontab commands
  • crontab -e: Edit current user's crontab; creates it if missing.
  • crontab -l: List current user's entries.
  • crontab -r: Remove current user's crontab.
  • crontab -u user -e: (root only) edit another user's crontab.
Don't edit files under /var/spool/cron/tabs directly; use the crontab utility so cron picks up changes safely.
Example entry
*/5 * * * * /home/$USER/cron_scripts/check_disk.sh >> /home/$USER/disk_usage.log 2>&1
This runs every five minutes and appends both stdout and stderr to a log for inspection.
Misconception
Saving a crontab with a syntax error may prevent cron from installing the changes; verify with crontab -l.
Check
After adding a job, wait the scheduled interval and inspect the redirected log to confirm execution.

screens.title: Understanding the five cron fields
screens.narratorSegment: A crontab entry uses five time-and-date fields followed by the command to run. Reading from left to right: minute (0–59), hour (0–23), day of month (1–31), month (1–12 or jan–dec), and day of week (0–7 or sun–sat, where 0 and 7 are both Sunday). An asterisk means every allowed value. You can provide ranges like 9-17 to specify working hours, lists such as Mon,Wed,Fri, or step values like */15 to run every 15 minutes. Example: 0 2 * * * runs daily at 2:00 AM, while 30 10 1,15 * 1-5 runs at 10:30 AM on the 1st and 15th but only if those dates are Monday through Friday. A misconception is believing that both day-of-month and day-of-week must match; in many implementations, cron treats them as a logical OR for historical reasons unless explicitly stated otherwise, which can be confusing. Always test a complex schedule by scheduling a short-lived command to confirm the behavior. Use comments in crontab to document non-obvious schedules. Being fluent with these fields lets you build precise recurring tasks without over-scheduling work. Understanding the five cron fields means master the five schedule fields, use ranges, lists, and steps, and test complex schedules to avoid surprises.. In practical terms, minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Syntax › The five cron fields explained
Field mapping
* * * * * command_to_execute - - - - - | | | | | | | | | ----- Day of week (0 - 7) | | | ------- Month (1 - 12) | | --------- Day of month (1 - 31) | ----------- Hour (0 - 23) ------------- Minute (0 - 59)
Use ranges, lists, and step values to express schedules succinctly.
Examples
0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh # daily at 02:00 */15 * * * * /usr/local/bin/short_task.sh # every 15 minutes 30 10 1,15 * 1-5 /path/to/command # 10:30 on the 1st and 15th, but only on weekdays
Misconception
Day-of-month and day-of-week logic can be non-intuitive; test complex expressions to confirm actual matches.
Pro tip
When debugging a schedule, temporarily set it to run every minute and observe behavior before restoring the intended timing.

screens.title: User crontab vs. system crontab
screens.narratorSegment: There are two primary scheduling approaches: user crontabs and system-wide cron configuration. A user crontab entry contains only the five schedule fields and the command. The system /etc/crontab format adds a sixth field: the user under which the command runs. For example, /etc/crontab uses: minute hour day month weekday user command. System files and the /etc/cron. d directory are managed by root and are suitable for OS and service maintenance. The /etc/cron. hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly directories contain executable scripts that run via run-parts on the corresponding schedule; scripts placed there must be executable and are run as configured in /etc/crontab. A common misconception is that adding files to /etc/cron. d uses the userless format; in fact, those files follow the /etc/crontab convention and require the user field. Use user crontabs for personal automation when possible to avoid cluttering system configuration, and reserve /etc entries for system-level maintenance where root privileges are appropriate. Always test system scripts manually and ensure their ownership and execute bits are correct before relying on automated runs. User crontab vs. system crontab means user crontabs omit a user field and are edited with crontab -e; system crontabs include the user field and are managed by root in /etc paths.. In practical terms, how formats and responsibilities differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › User crontab vs. system crontab
User crontab
Format: five fields + command. Edited with crontab -e. Runs with the owning user's privileges. Good for personal automation and tasks that do not need root.
# user crontab format */5 * * * * /home/user/cron_scripts/check_disk.sh >> /home/user/disk_usage.log 2>&1
System crontab (/etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d)
Format: five fields + user + command. Managed by root. Suitable for system maintenance and application-specific jobs.
# /etc/crontab example 0 3 * * * root /usr/bin/apt update >> /var/log/apt_daily.log 2>&1
cron.* directories
Place executable scripts in /etc/cron.hourly, /etc/cron.daily, /etc/cron.weekly, or /etc/cron.monthly. These are run by run-parts according to system schedule in /etc/crontab.

screens.title: Hands-on: create and schedule a disk-check script
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a hands-on example that maps directly to the chapter exercise. First, create a directory for cron scripts and an executable script that appends disk usage to a log. The script should begin with a shebang and use absolute commands such as df so cron can run it reliably. Next, make it executable with chmod +x. Then open your user crontab with crontab -e and add an entry that runs the script every five minutes, using a schedule like */5 * * * * and redirect both stdout and stderr to a log so you can inspect output. After saving, wait for the interval and check that /home/youruser/disk_usage. log contains new entries. If nothing appears, check that the cron daemon is running, confirm the script's execute permission, and ensure you used absolute paths. This example demonstrates the common flow: create, set execute, schedule, and verify. A common mistake is assuming ~ expansion inside crontab; use full paths instead of tilde or relative references. The core takeaway is to treat cron runs like remote execution: be explicit about everything.

keyIdea.text: Create an executable script with absolute paths, schedule it with crontab -e, redirect output to logs, and verify execution by checking the logs.

content.html:
Process Flow › Hands-on: create and schedule a disk-check script
Step-by-step commands
mkdir -p /home/$USER/cron_scripts
cat << EOF > /home/$USER/cron_scripts/check_disk.sh
#!/bin/bash
echo "Disk usage at $(date):" >> /home/$USER/disk_usage.log
df -h / >> /home/$USER/disk_usage.log
echo "---" >> /home/$USER/disk_usage.log
EOF
chmod +x /home/$USER/cron_scripts/check_disk.sh

# Edit crontab
crontab -e
# Add:
*/5 * * * * /home/$USER/cron_scripts/check_disk.sh >> /home/$USER/disk_usage.log 2>&1
Use the full path to the script and log file to avoid shell expansion and path resolution issues.
Example verification
After 5–10 minutes run: cat /home/$USER/disk_usage.log to inspect entries. Use tail -f to watch updates in real time.
Common mistake
Using ~ in crontab entries. Always write full absolute paths to files and executables.
Check your work
Confirm execute permissions and cron daemon status if logs are not updating.

screens.title: System-wide cron: /etc/crontab and cron.d
screens.narratorSegment: System-level scheduling is handled by files a privileged user manages. The primary system file, /etc/crontab, uses a six-field format that includes the user account the command should run as. This is convenient for maintenance tasks that must run with a specific privilege. Another mechanism is /etc/cron. d, a directory of files where packages or services place their crontab entries; these files use the same /etc/crontab format and must include the user field. Additionally, the cron. hourly, cron. daily, cron. weekly, and cron. monthly directories provide a simple way to schedule scripts at fixed intervals via run-parts. Scripts placed there must be executable and are run as configured in the system crontab. A practical example is adding a root job to /etc/crontab to run apt update every day at 03:00, capturing output to /var/log/apt_daily. log. Always test system scripts manually and ensure correct ownership and permissions before enabling them in cron. A frequent error is forgetting execute bits on scripts in cron. daily; the script will be ignored. The key lesson is to reserve system cron for tasks that require administrative privileges and to be meticulous about testing and logging.

System Cron › /etc/crontab and cron.d
/etc/crontab format
# minute hour day month weekday user command 0 3 * * * root /usr/bin/apt update >> /var/log/apt_daily.log 2>&1
This runs apt update at 03:00 as root and logs output. Files in /etc/cron.d follow this format as well.
cron.* directories
Scripts placed in /etc/cron.daily are run by run-parts at the configured time. Ensure scripts are executable and idempotent where possible.
# Example daily script sudo bash -c 'cat << EOF > /etc/cron.daily/daily_update #!/bin/bash LOGFILE="/var/log/daily_update.log" echo "Daily update started at $(date)" >> $LOGFILE apt update >> $LOGFILE 2>&1 echo "Daily update finished at $(date)" >> $LOGFILE EOF' sudo chmod +x /etc/cron.daily/daily_update
Common mistake
Placing a script in cron.daily without making it executable. run-parts will skip non-executable files.

screens.title: Environment variables and PATH issues
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most frequent sources of cron failures is the minimal environment provided when a job runs. Interactive shells set PATH, HOME, and other variables for convenience; cron typically starts commands with a stripped-down environment containing only a few variables. A script that runs manually may fail under cron because it cannot find commands like python or custom binaries. The remedy is simple: use absolute paths in scripts, set PATH at the top of your crontab or inside the script, and export any variables the script depends on. For example, adding PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin at the top of a crontab ensures commands are discoverable. Another option is to hard-code full paths to executables, for example /usr/bin/python instead of python. When diagnosing, redirect both stdout and stderr to a log and inspect it. A common misconception is that cron logs errors to syslog by default; unless the job explicitly sends output, cron mails the output to the user, which many systems do not deliver. Logging to a file is more reliable for debugging. Key takeaway: replicate the minimal cron environment when testing to reproduce failures quickly.

content.html:
Troubleshooting › Environment variables and PATH issues
Why this fails
Interactive shells configure PATH and other variables. Cron provides a small environment and will not find commands unless they are absolute or PATH is set.
# Set PATH at top of crontab PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
Alternatively, reference full paths within your script to guarantee correct binary resolution.
Diagnose with logging
Redirect stdout and stderr to a log file to capture errors cron would otherwise mail to the user.
*/5 * * * * /path/to/script.sh >> /var/log/script.log 2>&1
Misconception
Assuming cron mails are seen. Many systems don't deliver mail by default; logs are safer.
Practical tip
When replicating failures, run the script with env -i to mimic cron's minimal environment and reproduce issues quickly.

screens.title: Permissions, output redirection, and email
screens.narratorSegment: Permissions and output handling are practical concerns that determine whether cron jobs run successfully and whether you can diagnose issues. Always ensure the script file has execute permission — chmod +x script. sh — and that the user configured in crontab has appropriate rights to read or write files the script touches. If a cron job writes to a log under /var/log, the job must run as a user who can write there or the script must use sudo responsibly and securely. By default cron sends stdout and stderr to the user by mail; if the system does not deliver mail or you do not monitor it, errors will be missed. Redirect output to a log file using >> to append and 2>&1 to include stderr in the same file. To suppress output entirely, redirect to /dev/null. A common mistake is scheduling a script that writes to a log file in a directory where the cron user lacks write permissions. Always test writing as the cron user and check file ownership. Key takeaway: confirm execute permissions, use explicit redirection, and choose log locations that the cron user can access.

keyIdea.text: Make scripts executable, verify file ownership and permissions, and redirect output to writable logs to capture errors.

Permissions & Output › Ensure scripts can run and logs are accessible
Execute permissions
Set executable bit: chmod +x /path/to/script.sh. Verify ownership and that the cron user can access any files the script reads or writes.
Output redirection
# Append both stdout and stderr 0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1 # Suppress output 0 3 * * * /path/to/command > /dev/null 2>&1
Redirect to a log you control so you can inspect failures even if mail isn't configured.
Common mistake
Writing logs to a directory owned by root when the job runs under a non-root user. Ensure correct ownership or use root-managed logs carefully.

screens.title: Diagnosing a job that won't run
screens.narratorSegment: When a cron job doesn't run, follow a methodical checklist. First, verify the cron daemon is active with the system service manager: systemctl status cron or systemctl status crond depending on your distribution. Second, inspect the crontab entry for syntax errors and confirm it is present with crontab -l. Third, confirm execute permissions on the script and that absolute paths are used for binaries. Fourth, check PATH and other environment variables—either set PATH at the top of the crontab or use full paths inside the script. Fifth, examine output logs or redirect output to capture errors. Sixth, verify user access control via /etc/cron. allow or /etc/cron. deny; if cron. allow exists, the user must be listed there, and if only cron. deny exists, listed users are blocked. Finally, check for silent failures by running the script manually using the same user and environment as cron, or simulate cron with env -i to reproduce minimal environment conditions. A common trap is assuming cron sends visible mail; logs are more reliable. The diagnostic process narrows the fault quickly when applied in order.

keyIdea.text: Follow a fixed sequence: check daemon status, crontab syntax, permissions, environment, logging, and allow/deny controls to isolate failures.

content.html:
Troubleshooting › Diagnosing a job that won't run
Step-by-step checklist
  1. Check cron service: systemctl status cron or crond.
  2. Confirm crontab entry exists: crontab -l.
  3. Verify script execute permission and ownership.
  4. Ensure absolute paths or set PATH in crontab.
  5. Redirect stdout/stderr to a log and inspect it.
  6. Check /etc/cron.allow and /etc/cron.deny for user access control.
  7. Run the script manually as the cron user or use env -i to mimic cron's environment.
Quick debug
Temporarily set the schedule to run every minute and watch logs to speed up diagnosis.
Verification
After fixing, confirm the job runs on schedule and that logs show expected output.

screens.title: Scheduling as root and safety practices
screens.narratorSegment: Scheduling tasks as root is powerful but risky. A poorly written or untested script running with root privileges can modify system state, remove files, or create security issues. Before placing scripts into /etc/cron. daily or adding root entries to /etc/crontab, test the scripts thoroughly running them manually and confirm correct behavior and idempotence where possible. Limit the work run as root to only what requires those privileges; for other tasks, use a less-privileged user. When a root job needs elevated rights for specific commands, consider invoking sudo for a narrow set of commands from a controlled user script rather than running the entire script as root. Also, ensure logs and outputs are rotated and stored safely so they don't grow without bounds. Finally, keep clear comments in system crontab entries indicating purpose and maintenance instructions. The key safety habit is to treat scheduled root jobs with the same care as code deployed to production: test, document, and restrict privileges. Scheduling as root and safety practices means test root scripts thoroughly, minimize privileged operations, and document and log system cron tasks to avoid accidental system damage.. In practical terms, best practices and risks when automating with root privileges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
Automation saves time and reduces human error. In this lesson you will learn what the cron daemon does, how user and system crontabs differ, and practical rules for writing reliable cron jobs. We'll show concrete scripts and safe configuration patterns so you can schedule periodic tasks like disk checks, backups, and daily updates. You will also learn common pitfalls — missing PATH entries, permission issues, and where cron sends output — and how to troubleshoot them by redirecting logs and checking the cron service. By the end, you'll be able to create a user cron job for frequent checks, install a system-wide daily script, and verify that the scheduled tasks actually run. This knowledge matters because automation runs without interactive oversight; a small mistake in a scheduled job can fail silently or, when run as root, cause widespread problems. Think of cron as a simple scheduler with strict rules: give it absolute paths, explicit environment settings, and clear logging. As you proceed, practice the hands-on scenario to build confidence. What simple, repeatable task would you automate first on your system?

These objectives focus your practice for scheduling with cron. First, you'll understand the purpose and architecture of the cron daemon so you can reason about when and how jobs run. Second, you'll create and manage user-specific crontab entries using the crontab command, allowing you to automate tasks without touching system files. Third, you'll configure system-wide cron jobs by editing /etc/crontab and placing scripts in the cron.* directories for predictable, system-level maintenance. Finally, you'll troubleshoot common cron issues: environment variables and PATH, file permissions, output redirection, and how cron's minimal runtime can cause scripts to behave differently than in an interactive shell. Each objective is paired with a practical milestone so you can verify competency by running a scheduled check or deploying a daily script. These skills matter because automated tasks often run unattended; understanding both formats and typical failure modes prevents silent errors and keeps systems healthy.

Practical practice cements cron skills. You will: create a simple shell script that logs disk usage, schedule it to run every five minutes from your user crontab, and verify output is appended to a file. Then, as root, you will install a small daily update script into /etc/cron. daily and run it manually to confirm behavior. Each step tests a different part of cron: user crontab editing tools, filesystem permissions and execute bits, and system-level scheduling via run-parts. Use absolute command paths in both scripts and add explicit PATH definitions in crontab when needed. Capture output with redirection so you can inspect what cron produced. These exercises teach you to confirm a job ran and to diagnose why one might not have. After completing these milestones you will be able to demonstrate a scheduled job, read its log, and explain how to fix the top three causes of cron failures.

Cron is a background scheduler: a lightweight daemon that checks configured crontab entries and launches commands at the scheduled times. The daemon, often started as cron or crond by the system service manager, repeatedly examines crontab files and directories to determine which jobs should run. A job can be defined in a user crontab or in system locations like /etc/crontab, /etc/cron. d, or the cron.* directories. When cron decides a job should run, it invokes the command with a limited environment. That reduced environment is a frequent source of surprises: command names and environment variables you rely on in an interactive shell may not exist under cron. A concrete example is a backup script that runs fine when you execute it manually, but fails in cron because the script calls python without the full PATH; cron cannot find python. A common misconception is that cron inherits your full login environment — it does not. You must either use absolute program paths or explicitly set PATH and other needed variables in the crontab or inside the script. Key takeaway: cron starts jobs reliably, but you must control the environment and permissions so those jobs run as you expect.

Each user can maintain their own crontab file using the crontab utility; you should not edit files in /var/spool/cron/tabs directly. The key commands are crontab -e to edit (which creates the crontab if missing), crontab -l to list entries, and crontab -r to remove the current user's crontab. As root you may use crontab -u username -e to edit another user's crontab. A safe editing workflow is to run crontab -e, add your entry using absolute paths and explicit redirection for logs, then save. Verify with crontab -l and inspect any log files you redirected output into. A common misconception is that crontab -e uses your preferred editor without checks; it does, but a syntax error in a saved crontab can stop jobs from being installed, so always validate the entry format. Example: adding */5 * * * * /home/user/cron_scripts/check_disk. sh will run the script every five minutes. After editing, check the log file after 5–10 minutes to confirm that the job executed, and if it did not, check PATH, permissions, and the cron daemon status. This process gives you control over per-user automation without root access to system crontabs.

A crontab entry uses five time-and-date fields followed by the command to run. Reading from left to right: minute (0–59), hour (0–23), day of month (1–31), month (1–12 or jan–dec), and day of week (0–7 or sun–sat, where 0 and 7 are both Sunday). An asterisk means every allowed value. You can provide ranges like 9-17 to specify working hours, lists such as Mon,Wed,Fri, or step values like */15 to run every 15 minutes. Example: 0 2 * * * runs daily at 2:00 AM, while 30 10 1,15 * 1-5 runs at 10:30 AM on the 1st and 15th but only if those dates are Monday through Friday. A misconception is believing that both day-of-month and day-of-week must match; in many implementations, cron treats them as a logical OR for historical reasons unless explicitly stated otherwise, which can be confusing. Always test a complex schedule by scheduling a short-lived command to confirm the behavior. Use comments in crontab to document non-obvious schedules. Being fluent with these fields lets you build precise recurring tasks without over-scheduling work. Understanding the five cron fields means master the five schedule fields, use ranges, lists, and steps, and test complex schedules to avoid surprises.. In practical terms, minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are two primary scheduling approaches: user crontabs and system-wide cron configuration. A user crontab entry contains only the five schedule fields and the command. The system /etc/crontab format adds a sixth field: the user under which the command runs. For example, /etc/crontab uses: minute hour day month weekday user command. System files and the /etc/cron. d directory are managed by root and are suitable for OS and service maintenance. The /etc/cron. hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly directories contain executable scripts that run via run-parts on the corresponding schedule; scripts placed there must be executable and are run as configured in /etc/crontab. A common misconception is that adding files to /etc/cron. d uses the userless format; in fact, those files follow the /etc/crontab convention and require the user field. Use user crontabs for personal automation when possible to avoid cluttering system configuration, and reserve /etc entries for system-level maintenance where root privileges are appropriate. Always test system scripts manually and ensure their ownership and execute bits are correct before relying on automated runs. User crontab vs. system crontab means user crontabs omit a user field and are edited with crontab -e; system crontabs include the user field and are managed by root in /etc paths.. In practical terms, how formats and responsibilities differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a hands-on example that maps directly to the chapter exercise. First, create a directory for cron scripts and an executable script that appends disk usage to a log. The script should begin with a shebang and use absolute commands such as df so cron can run it reliably. Next, make it executable with chmod +x. Then open your user crontab with crontab -e and add an entry that runs the script every five minutes, using a schedule like */5 * * * * and redirect both stdout and stderr to a log so you can inspect output. After saving, wait for the interval and check that /home/youruser/disk_usage. log contains new entries. If nothing appears, check that the cron daemon is running, confirm the script's execute permission, and ensure you used absolute paths. This example demonstrates the common flow: create, set execute, schedule, and verify. A common mistake is assuming ~ expansion inside crontab; use full paths instead of tilde or relative references. The core takeaway is to treat cron runs like remote execution: be explicit about everything.

System-level scheduling is handled by files a privileged user manages. The primary system file, /etc/crontab, uses a six-field format that includes the user account the command should run as. This is convenient for maintenance tasks that must run with a specific privilege. Another mechanism is /etc/cron. d, a directory of files where packages or services place their crontab entries; these files use the same /etc/crontab format and must include the user field. Additionally, the cron. hourly, cron. daily, cron. weekly, and cron. monthly directories provide a simple way to schedule scripts at fixed intervals via run-parts. Scripts placed there must be executable and are run as configured in the system crontab. A practical example is adding a root job to /etc/crontab to run apt update every day at 03:00, capturing output to /var/log/apt_daily. log. Always test system scripts manually and ensure correct ownership and permissions before enabling them in cron. A frequent error is forgetting execute bits on scripts in cron. daily; the script will be ignored. The key lesson is to reserve system cron for tasks that require administrative privileges and to be meticulous about testing and logging.

Interactive shells set PATH, HOME, and other variables for convenience; cron typically starts commands with a stripped-down environment containing only a few variables. For example, adding PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin at the top of a crontab ensures commands are discoverable. Another option is to hard-code full paths to executables, for example /usr/bin/python instead of python. When diagnosing, redirect both stdout and stderr to a log and inspect it. A common misconception is that cron logs errors to syslog by default; unless the job explicitly sends output, cron mails the output to the user, which many systems do not deliver. Logging to a file is more reliable for debugging. Key takeaway: replicate the minimal cron environment when testing to reproduce failures quickly.

By default cron sends stdout and stderr to the user by mail; if the system does not deliver mail or you do not monitor it, errors will be missed. Redirect output to a log file using >> to append and 2>&1 to include stderr in the same file. To suppress output entirely, redirect to /dev/null. A common mistake is scheduling a script that writes to a log file in a directory where the cron user lacks write permissions. Always test writing as the cron user and check file ownership. Key takeaway: confirm execute permissions, use explicit redirection, and choose log locations that the cron user can access.

When a cron job doesn't run, follow a methodical checklist. First, verify the cron daemon is active with the system service manager: systemctl status cron or systemctl status crond depending on your distribution. Second, inspect the crontab entry for syntax errors and confirm it is present with crontab -l. Third, confirm execute permissions on the script and that absolute paths are used for binaries. Finally, check for silent failures by running the script manually using the same user and environment as cron, or simulate cron with env -i to reproduce minimal environment conditions. A common trap is assuming cron sends visible mail; logs are more reliable. The diagnostic process narrows the fault quickly when applied in order.

Scheduling tasks as root is powerful but risky. A poorly written or untested script running with root privileges can modify system state, remove files, or create security issues. Before placing scripts into /etc/cron. daily or adding root entries to /etc/crontab, test the scripts thoroughly running them manually and confirm correct behavior and idempotence where possible. Limit the work run as root to only what requires those privileges; for other tasks, use a less-privileged user. When a root job needs elevated rights for specific commands, consider invoking sudo for a narrow set of commands from a controlled user script rather than running the entire script as root. Also, ensure logs and outputs are rotated and stored safely so they don't grow without bounds. Finally, keep clear comments in system crontab entries indicating purpose and maintenance instructions. The key safety habit is to treat scheduled root jobs with the same care as code deployed to production: test, document, and restrict privileges.
